topic_title: Top 5 Dog Breeds That Love Swimming
intro: A dog that loves water was usually bred to retrieve from it. That shows in the body: a dense or water-resistant coat, a strong tail for steering, and often webbed toes. It also shows in the routine. Water dogs need a lot of exercise, their coats need drying and brushing after every swim to prevent hot spots, and floppy ears need cleaning to avoid infections. Even natural swimmers should wear a dog life jacket in open water or boats.

picks.description: The Standard Poodle began as a German water retriever; the name comes from the German word for splashing. Its curly, dense coat sheds very little, which makes it the best swimming option on this list for people who dislike dog hair, though no breed is fully allergy-free. The trade-off is grooming: daily or near-daily brushing and a professional trim every four to eight weeks, plus thorough drying after swims to prevent matting. Standards are highly intelligent, easy to train, athletic and good with children and other pets. They need about an hour of exercise and mental work daily. Smaller Miniature and Toy Poodles share the coat but not the size or swimming stamina.
picks.best_for: Owners wanting a low-shedding, very trainable swimming dog
picks.quirky_fact: The traditional poodle show clip began as a practical cut for swimming dogs, leaving fur over the joints and chest for warmth.
picks.skip_if: You can't budget time or money for regular professional grooming

picks.description: The Toller is the smallest retriever, around 35 to 50 pounds, bred in Nova Scotia to lure ducks within range by playing at the water's edge and then retrieve them. It has a medium-length, water-resistant double coat that sheds moderately and needs weekly brushing. Energy is high: plan on 60 to 90 minutes of activity a day, with swimming, retrieving and training games to keep its busy mind occupied. Tollers are smart, easy to train and good with families, cats and other dogs, but under-exercised ones get noisy, including a high-pitched 'Toller scream' when excited. A good pick for active people who want retriever drive in a more compact dog.
picks.best_for: Active owners wanting retriever drive in a medium-sized dog
picks.quirky_fact: Tollers are famous for a high-pitched excited scream, which surprises new owners.
picks.skip_if: You want a calm couch dog or can't offer daily vigorous exercise

picks.description: The Newfoundland is a giant working dog, often 100 to 150 pounds, bred to haul nets and rescue people from cold water. Webbed feet, a heavy water-resistant coat and a strong swimming stroke make it the most natural lifesaver on this list. Energy is moderate: daily walks and swims rather than running, which suits calmer households. The trade-offs are size and coat. Newfies shed heavily, need brushing several times a week, and drool, especially after drinking. They are gentle, patient with children and good with other pets. Their lifespan is shorter than average, around 8 to 10 years, and they need space, a car that fits them and a budget for giant-dog food and vet care.
picks.best_for: Calm households with space wanting a gentle giant swimmer
picks.quirky_fact: Newfoundlands have a long history of water rescue work and are still trained for it in some countries.
picks.skip_if: You dislike drool, live in a small space, or want a long-lived dog

picks.description: The Labrador Retriever traces back to Newfoundland fishing dogs that hauled nets and retrieved from icy water. Its short, dense double coat sheds water quickly and needs less grooming than a Golden's, though it still sheds a lot. The otter-like tail works as a rudder. Labs need about an hour of real exercise daily, and many will swim until they are exhausted, so set limits. They are among the easiest breeds to train, good with children, cats and other dogs, and eager to please. Expect a big appetite: Labs are prone to weight gain, so measured meals matter. A Lab that is under-exercised often chews and jumps.
picks.best_for: First-time and family owners wanting an easy-to-train water dog
picks.quirky_fact: Labs are known for food motivation, which makes training easy and makes measured meals important.
picks.skip_if: You want a low-shedding dog or can't commit to daily exercise

picks.description: The Golden Retriever was bred in Scotland to retrieve shot birds from land and water, and most still treat a lake as a reward. The dense, water-repellent double coat dries slowly and sheds heavily year-round, with bigger seasonal drops, so plan on brushing several times a week and a thorough dry after every swim. Energy is high: about an hour of exercise a day, and swimming is an easy way to deliver it. Goldens are easy to train, gentle with children and usually friendly with cats and other dogs. They thrive on company and can become destructive if left alone for long days. Their size, around 55 to 75 pounds, suits a house better than a small apartment.
picks.best_for: Active families who want a gentle, trainable swimming companion
picks.quirky_fact: Goldens have a soft mouth, bred to carry birds without damage, which is why many will carry toys around the house.
picks.skip_if: You can't handle heavy shedding or leave the dog alone most of the day

faqs.question: Which dog breeds are the best swimmers?
faqs.answer: Breeds developed to retrieve from water are the strongest swimmers: Labrador and Golden Retrievers, Newfoundlands, Portuguese Water Dogs, Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retrievers, Chesapeake Bay Retrievers and Standard Poodles. Most have water-resistant coats and many have webbed feet. Individual dogs still vary, so introduce water gradually.

faqs.question: Do all dogs know how to swim?
faqs.answer: No. Many dogs paddle instinctively but tire fast or panic, and breeds with heavy chests, short legs or flat faces, such as Bulldogs, Pugs and Dachshunds, struggle to stay afloat. Use a dog life jacket and start in shallow, calm water.

faqs.question: How do I teach my dog to swim?
faqs.answer: Start in shallow, calm water where the dog can stand, ideally wearing a properly fitted life jacket. Walk in with them, reward calm behavior, and let them choose to go deeper. Keep the first sessions to a few minutes and always show them where the exit is.

faqs.question: Is swimming good exercise for dogs?
faqs.answer: Yes. Swimming builds fitness without the impact of running, which makes it useful for large breeds and dogs with joint problems. Fifteen to twenty minutes of swimming can tire a dog as much as a much longer walk. Rinse off chlorine or salt water afterward.

faqs.question: How do I care for my dog's coat and ears after swimming?
faqs.answer: Rinse with fresh water, towel dry, and brush through dense coats so moisture is not trapped against the skin, which can cause hot spots. Dry the inside of floppy ears with a soft cloth or an ear-drying solution recommended by your vet to reduce the risk of ear infections.

seo_title: 5 Dog Breeds That Love Swimming (2026 Guide)
answer: The Golden Retriever, Labrador Retriever and Newfoundland are the most reliable swimmers here, all bred to work in water and built with water-resistant coats. Pick by size and energy: retrievers for active families, the Newfoundland for a calm giant, the Toller or Standard Poodle for a smaller or lower-shedding option.
method: We filtered a 150-breed dataset for breeds originally developed for water work, then ordered them by swimming ability and noted energy, shedding, grooming and family-compatibility traits so you can match one to your routine.
